items.title: Hierarchical Conditional Continuous Normalizing Flows for Creaky Voice Editing under Speaker Identity Preservation
items.authors: Frederik Rautenberg(Paderborn University); Fritz Seebauer(Bielefeld University); Petra Wagner(Bielefeld University); Reinhold Haeb-Umbach(Paderborn University)
items.abstract: We propose a hierarchical conditional continuous normalizing flow that structurally disentangles high-level speaker attributes from low-level paralinguistic voice qualities. By introducing a controlled, stage-wise injection of conditioning information, the model constrains how different feature types influence the latent representation. This design reduces unintended interactions between attributes and limits the propagation of low-level manipulations to high-level characteristics. Using the example of manipulating the voice quality creak, we show that the hierarchical approach has significantly less impact on the high-level speaker attributes pitch and gender, leading to improved preservation of perceived speaker identity.

items.title: TC-DBI: A Plug-and-Play Trajectory Confidence-Guided Dynamic Block Inference Strategy for Speech Synthesis with Continuous Block Flow Matching
items.authors: Ren Wang(Tsinghua University); Zhiyu Cui(Ant Group); Shun Lei(Tsinghua University); Jiawei Jin(Tsinghua University); Dongfu Song(Tsinghua University); Zhiyong Wu(Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University)
items.abstract: Block Flow Matching combines block-level autoregression with intra-block parallelism for efficient and high-quality Text-to-Speech (TTS). However, using a fixed block size during inference ignores the non-uniform modeling difficulty of speech, which can cause unstable velocity estimation in challenging regions. This motivates the need for a reliability metric that can guide dynamic adjustment of block size. We propose Trajectory Confidence (TC), a geometric measure derived from trajectory straightness during ODE integration, and introduce TC-Guided Dynamic Block Inference (TC-DBI), a plug-and-play strategy that truncates and regenerates unreliable regions to adapt block size without architectural changes. Experiments show that TC correlates strongly with generation errors, and TC-DBI improves robustness and perceptual quality while maintaining comparable efficiency. Audio samples are available at https://thuhcsi.github.io/ interspeech2026-TC-DBI/.

items.title: Bridging the Gap: A Hierarchical Framework for Cross-Modal Style Modeling in Expressive TTS
items.authors: Jiale Chen(Zhejiang University); Jiaxun Li(Zhejiang University); Wei Li(Zhejiang University); Yuanpeng Wang(Zhejiang University); Yuehai Wang(Zhejiang University)
items.abstract: Natural language prompts offer a highly flexible interface for expressive text-to-speech (TTS), yet cross-modal gaps and one-to-many mapping problem hinder reliable style control. To address this, we propose OTAFlow, a novel hierarchical cross-modal style modeling framework. First, optimal transport alignment, contrastive learning, and multi-task supervision are jointly optimized to construct a unified style space that preserves instance-level correspondence and expressive factor separability. Second, a conditional flow matching module is introduced to capture the residual modality gap, explicitly addressing the one-to-many challenge by generating diverse acoustic style embeddings from a single prompt. When plugged into a downstream TTS backbone, evaluations show that our method substantially outperforms baseline models in fine-grained style retrieval and synthesized style accuracy, effectively delivering diverse and controllable expressive speech. Audio samples can be found in our demo page.

items.title: RobustSpeechFlow: Learning Robust Text-to-Speech Trajectories via Augmentation-based Contrastive Flow Matching
items.authors: Jinhyeok Yang(Supertone Inc.); Hyeongju Kim(Out of Set Inc.); Yechan Yu(Supertone Inc.); Joon Byun(Supertone Inc.); Frederik Bous(Supertone Inc.); Juheon Lee(Supertone Inc.)
items.abstract: While flow-matching text-to-speech (TTS) achieves strong zero-shot speaker similarity and naturalness, it remains susceptible to content fidelity issues, particularly skip and repeat errors from imperfect alignment. We propose RobustSpeechFlow, a training strategy that improves alignment robustness by extending contrastive flow matching with length-preserving repeat and skip latent augmentations. Requiring no external aligners or preference data, our method directly penalizes realistic failure modes and readily integrates into existing pipelines. On Seed-TTS-eval, it reduces the word error rate (WER) from 1.44 to 1.38 using only 0.06B parameters. On our ZERO500 benchmark, it delivers consistent intelligibility improvements across diverse speaker and prosody conditions; at NFE=24, it reduces English character error rate (CER) from 0.48% to 0.35% and Korean CER from 0.81% to 0.57%. Audio samples: https://robustspeechflow.github.io/.

items.title: Improving Flow Matching based Text-to-Speech with Dual-Model Preference Optimization and Classifier-Free Guidance
items.authors: Minchuan Chen(Ping An Technology); Chenchen Wan(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Junjie Li(Ping An Technology); Peng Qi(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Shaojun Wang(Ping An Technology); Jing Xiao(Ping An Technology)
items.abstract: Flow matching is a powerful generative model and has become a core component of modern text-to-speech (TTS) systems. In order to ensure high-quality speech synthesis, Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is widely used during the training and inference stages of flow matching based TTS models. However, in zero-shot TTS, conventional training and inference paradigms typically cannot effectively integrate human feedback, resulting in a mismatch between training objectives and evaluation metrics. In this work, we propose a preference optimization method by separately modeling preferred and dispreferred information with two distinct models, which enables better utilization of preferred and dispreferred data. We further incorporate an improved CFG technique to enhance synthesis adherence to the text and reference audio. Experiments demonstrate that these optimizations significantly enhance intelligibility, speaker similarity and naturalness of synthesized speech, outperforming the baseline model.

items.title: Enhancing Flow Matching with A Unified Guidance Framework for Efficient and Robust Speech Synthesis
items.authors: Zuda Yu(Zuoyebang); Qianhui Xu(Zuoyebang); Ting Chen(Zuoyebang); Junhui Zhang(Zuoyebang); Tao Fu(Zuoyebang); Hongjiang Yu(Zuoyebang); Qiangqiang Wang(Zuoyebang); Yang Song(Zuoyebang)
items.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for speech generation but remains constrained by high inference latency and timbre leakage. To address these bottlenecks, we propose a unified guidance framework that enhances generation efficiency and robustness through two complementary strategies. On the data front, we introduce Data-guidance via heterogeneous augmentation, encouraging the model to disentangle linguistic content from acoustic residue. In parallel, we propose an enhanced Model-guidance mechanism that synergizes trajectory rectification with a novel intrinsic guidance objective. This approach distills conditional knowledge into network weights and straightens inference trajectory path, thereby eliminating Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) overhead. Experiments demonstrate that our framework accelerates inference by nearly three times while effectively improving speaker similarity compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Audio samples are available here.

items.title: AppTek Call-Center Dialogues: A Multi-Accent Long-Form Benchmark for English ASR
items.authors: Eugen Beck(AppTek.ai); Sarah Beranek(AppTek.ai); Uma Moothiringote(AppTek.ai); Daniel Mann(AppTek.ai); Wilfried Michel(AppTek.ai); Katie Nguyen(AppTek.ai); Taylor Tragemann(AppTek.ai)
items.abstract: Evaluating English ASR systems for conversational AI applications remains difficult, as many publicly available corpora are either pre-segmented into short segments, consist of read or prepared speech, or lack explicit dialect annotations to evaluate robustness for a diverse user base. This work presents the AppTek Call-Center Dialogues corpus, a collection of spontaneous, role-played agent-customer conversations spanning fourteen English accents covering sixteen service-oriented scenarios. The dataset was commissioned specifically for evaluation and none of the audio or text was publicly available prior to release, reducing the risk of overlap with existing large-scale pretraining corpora. We benchmark a set of open-source ASR systems under different segmentation approaches. Results show substantial variation across accents and segmentation methods, indicating that good performance on general American English benchmarks does not necessarily generalize to other accents.

items.title: Segmental Attention Decoding With Long Form Acoustic Encodings
items.authors: Pawel Swietojanski(Apple); Xinwei Li(Apple); Mingbin Xu(Apple); Takaaki Hori(Apple); Dogan Can(Apple); Xiaodan Zhuang(Apple)
items.abstract: We address the fundamental incompatibility of attention-based encoder-decoder (AED) models with long-form acoustic encodings. AED trained on segmented utterances learn to encode absolute positions by exploiting limited acoustic context beyond segment boundaries, but fail to generalize when decoding long-form segments where these cues vanish. The model loses ability to order acoustic encodings due to permutation invariance of keys and values in cross-attention. We propose four modifications: 1) injecting explicit absolute positional encodings into cross-attention, 2) long-form training with extended acoustic context to eliminate implicit absolute position encoding, 3) segment concatenation to cover diverse segmentations needed during training, 4) semantic segmentation to align AED-decoded segments with training segments. We show that these modifications close the accuracy gap between continuous and segmented acoustic encodings, enabling auto-regressive use of the attention decoder.

items.title: M-LAMA: Multimodal Automated Scoring of Long-form Spoken English
items.authors: Minh Dao-Xuan-Quang(HUST); Son Dinh-Nguyen(Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Hanoi, VietNam); Thi-Mai-Anh Bui(Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Hanoi, VietNam); Phi-Le Nguyen(Hanoi University of Science and Technology, Hanoi, VietNam)
items.abstract: Automatic speech assessment (ASA) for real-world exams requires evaluating multi-minute spontaneous responses across acoustic delivery, linguistic quality, and task fulfillment. However, most prior work focuses on short utterances, leaving long-form comprehensive assessment underexplored. We investigate whether reliable scoring of extended speech requires structured multimodal modeling. We propose M-LAMA, a cross-modal framework integrating raw audio, ASR transcripts, and question context through dual encoders and a discourse-aware fusion decoder. A part-based audio structure and question-aware text encoding capture both how and what is spoken, while a three-stage training strategy addresses the bell-curve score distribution of high-stakes exams. Experiments on 87,226 full-length sessions show that structured multimodal alignment substantially improves scoring reliability across five criteria, suggesting that effective long-form ASA requires principled integration of acoustic, linguistic, and contextual evidence.

items.title: Attentive Mamba: Channel-wise Local Attention for Speech Recognition
items.authors: Jen-Tzung Chien(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Fan-Che Feng(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Ching-Hsien Lee(Industrial Technology Research Institute)
items.abstract: State space models (SSMs) have emerged as a powerful alternative to transformers for speech recognition, but the performance is constrained due to static local aggregation. This paper presents an attentive SSM that integrates a causal convolutional attention where the static convolution is upgraded with a channel-wise local attention. The proposed module first contextualizes queries, keys, and values via causal depth-wise convolutions before applying cross-channel attention over a temporally local window. This architecture is motivated by the inherent structure of speech spectrograms, where distinct frequency channels contain temporally coherent patterns that can benefit the channel-specific modeling prior to their integration. This design facilitates dynamic parameterization of the state transition matrices, leading to the expressive acoustic features. Experimental results confirm the merit of integrating dynamic channel-wise attention into SSM for speech recognition.

items.title: Attention-Guided Reliability Scaling for Contrastive Decoding in Robust Audio-Visual Speech Recognition
items.authors: YoungChae Kim(Hanyang University); Da-Hee Yang(Hanyang University); Joon-Hyuk Chang(Hanyang University)
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based audio-visual speech recognition (AVSR) systems are robust under noise. Contrastive decoding (CD), originally introduced to stabilize LLM generation by contrasting a weaker model against a stronger one at inference time, adjusts predictions without additional training. In this work, we apply CD to AVSR by contrasting audio-only conditioning with full audio-visual conditioning within the same underlying model. However, using a fixed contrastive strength introduces a trade-off across noise levels: stronger intervention helps under severe noise but may over-correct reliable predictions in clean conditions. We propose reliability-aware scaling of CD for AVSR. Instead of using a fixed strength, we adaptively modulate the contrastive influence at each token based on reliability signals derived from attention dynamics and inter-model predictive divergence. Experiments on LRS3 show consistent improvements across clean and low-SNR conditions.

items.title: Listening with Attention: Entropy-Guided Explainability for Transformer-Based Audio Models
items.authors: Ravi Kumar(Florida International University); Utkarsh Grover(University of South Florida); Xiaomin Lin(University of South Florida); Agoritsa Polyzou(Florida International University)
items.abstract: Transformer-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) models such as Whisper are highly accurate, but their predictions remain difficult to interpret. Existing explainable AI (XAI) methods often lack faithfulness and precise temporal grounding. We propose Listening with Entropy-guided Attention for Faithful eXplainability (LEAF-X), a model-intrinsic XAI framework for transformer-based ASR. LEAF-X combines entropy-guided attention weighting, multi-layer attention rollout, and optional causal ablations to identify low-entropy, high-impact heads and layers, producing sparse token-to-frame attributions. Unlike perturbation-based explainers or raw attention maps, LEAF-X exploits the internal structure of encoder-decoder and speech-augmented decoder-only models to generate explanations that better reflect model computation. Results show that LEAF-X produces more faithful and stable attributions than strong baselines, supporting more transparent and auditable ASR.

Adaptive AVSR: Integrating Speaker and Environmental Embeddings for Robust Audio-Visual Speech Recognition
items.authors: Christopher Simic(Technische Hochschule Nuernberg); Korbinian Riedhammer(Technische Hochschule Nuernberg); Tobias Bocklet(Technische Hochschule Nuernberg)
items.abstract: This work introduces adaptive mechanisms that integrate speaker and environmental noise embeddings into Audio-Visual Speech Recognition (AVSR) systems. Our approach extends a Whisper ASR model by an AV fusion module and incorporates speaker and noise scenario specific embeddings, which are extracted from the audio input samples. While we develop a custom attention-based model for noise embedding generation, we rely on X-Vector embeddings for speaker adaptation and evaluate three integration strategies: prefix concatenation, additional cross-attention layers and gated weighting. Noise embeddings are injected into the audio-visual fusion module while speaker embeddings are incorporated at the pre-decoder level. Evaluation on LRS3 across various noise conditions demonstrate gains of 3.5% for noise and 3.2% for speaker adaptation over our baseline. Compared to SOTA approach AV-HuBERT our models achieve relative WER reductions of up to 13.4%.

items.title: VIB-AVSR: Variational Information Bottleneck for Noise-Robust LLM-Based Audio-Visual Speech Recognition
items.authors: Piyush Arora(Imperial College London); Navlika Singh(Imperial College London); Umberto Cappellazzo(Imperial College London); Stavros Petridis(Imperial College London; NatWest AI Research); Maja Pantic(Imperial College London; NatWest AI Research)
items.abstract: Audio-Visual Speech Recognition takes two input modalities, acoustic and visual streams, where visual information from lip movements aids recognition when audio is noisy. Recently, LLM-based AVSR models have emerged as a promising paradigm by connecting pre-trained audio-visual encoders to an LLM, achieving strong results in clean conditions. However, these models are predominantly optimized for clean acoustic conditions, with limited attention to making the LLM backbone robust to noise. No explicit mechanism is employed to produce stable representations under corrupted audio, leading to performance degradation in noisy environments. To address this, we propose VIB-AVSR, which integrates Variational Information Bottleneck layers at targeted positions within the LLM backbone to regularize representations. VIB-AVSR reduces degradation under noisy conditions across multiple SNR levels and noise types, without requiring architectural modifications or additional training data. The implementation code is publicly available for reproducibility at Github repository.

items.title: Robust LLM-based Audio-Visual Speech Recognition with Sparse Modality Alignment and Visual Unit-Guided Refinement
items.authors: Fei Su(Wuhan University); Cancan Li(Wuhan University); Juan Liu(Wuhan University); Wei Ju(OPPO); Hongbin Suo(OPPO); Ming Li(The Chinese University of Hong Kong; Wuhan University)
items.abstract: Audio-Visual Speech Recognition (AVSR) integrates acoustic and visual information to enhance robustness in adverse acoustic conditions. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have yielded competitive automatic speech recognition performance and shown effectiveness for AVSR. However, prior approaches project audio and visual features independently or apply shallow fusion, limiting cross-modal alignment and complementary exchange while increasing the LLM's computational load. To address this, we propose AVUR-LLM, an LLM-based Audio-Visual Speech Recognition via Sparse Modality Alignment and Visual Unit-Guided Refinement. Experiments on LRS3 demonstrate state-of-the-art results for AVSR. Under additive-noise conditions at 0 dB SNR, it achieves 37% relative improvement over the baseline system. We release the AVUR-LLM code and related resources.1

items.title: MTC-AVSR: Compressed-Token-based Audio-Visual Speech Recognition and Translation with Contrastive Language Alignment
items.authors: Lusi A(Inner Mongolia University; National Local Joint Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Information Processing Technology for Mongolian; Inner Mongolia Key Laboratory of Multilingual Artificial Intelligence Technology); Zhiyong Duan(Inner Mongolia Arts University); Jiang Li(Inner Mongolia University; National Local Joint Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Information Processing Technology for Mongolian; Inner Mongolia Key Laboratory of Multilingual Artificial Intelligence Technology); Feilong Bao(Inner Mongolia University; National Local Joint Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Information Processing Technology for Mongolian; Inner Mongolia Key Laboratory of Multilingual Artificial Intelligence Technology)
items.abstract: Audio-visual speech recognition (AVSR) has achieved robust accuracy by fusing lip motion with acoustic cues; however, state-of-the-art systems still rely on high-resolution multimodal sequences, imposing prohibitive computational costs on large language models. Recent attempts to compress tokens remain confined to single-task recognition. We address the open question of whether the same compressed tokens can simultaneously support speech recognition and speech-to-text translation without retraining the encoder. We propose MTC-AVSR, a multi-task model built upon minimal multimodal speech (MMS) tokens. The framework couples an MMS-style token compressor with a prompt-conditioned LLM for single-stream inference, introduces a lightweight language adapter module (LAM) that maps compressed, source-aligned tokens into multilingual representations, and presents the token-contrastive alignment loss (TCAL) to align adapter outputs with a multilingual lexicon via contrastive learning. Experiments show that our model achieves a word error rate (WER) of 0.74% on LRS3 (on par with SOTA) while setting new records on MuAViC En-X tasks: English-Spanish BLEU 28.1, French BLEU 26.3, and Portuguese BLEU 21.8, all state-of-the-art, validating the residual linguistic capacity of compressed tokens under joint audio-visual speech recognition and translation scenarios.

items.title: Adaptive Turn-Taking for Real-time Multi-Party Voice Agents
items.authors: Soumyajit Mitra(Amazon AGI); Prabhat Pandey(Amazon AGI); Abhinav Jain(Amazon AGI); Shanmukha Sahith(IIT Kharagpur); K V Vijay Girish(Amazon AGI)
items.abstract: Turn-taking in multi-party spoken conversations remains a fundamental challenge for voice-based agents, particularly under dynamic floor competition and varying user expectations. We propose ModeratorLM, a role-playing voice agent that conditions turn-taking behavior on an explicitly assigned role in multi-party settings. The system is built on a speech large language model operating in chunk-wise streaming manner. We further introduce a reasoning-augmented variant that incorporates chain-of-thought reasoning over conversational context and the assigned role. We construct RolePlayConv, a large-scale synthetic dataset of spoken multi-party conversations with diverse assistant roles. Experiments on real-world meeting data and RolePlayConv show improved turn-taking precision by over 40% and recall by more than 70%, while substantially reducing false-positive interruptions compared to non-role-conditioned baselines.

items.title: Before the Turn: Investigating Motion Cues Preceding Speech in Dyadic Interaction
items.authors: Ying-Hsuan Huang(National Tsing Hua University); Woan-Shiuan Chien(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Huan-Yu Chen(National Tsing Hua University); Chi-Chun Lee(National Tsing Hua University)
items.abstract: Smooth turn-taking is essential for natural interaction in face-to-face spoken dialogue. However, reactive models often lag and fail to account for asynchronous pre-speech motion onsets across body parts. Our work presents a systematic analysis to determine the effect of continuous kinematics on predictive lead times as one of the first to adopt this perspective. Specifically, we evaluate a Transformer on InterAct 3D skeletal data by varying observation windows and lead times across diverse scenarios. Moreover, our results indicate that intent operates on independent timelines where upper-body signals enable stable predictions up to 3.0s prior to speech, while turn-claiming involves a 1.5s preparatory build-up versus the explosive burst of floor-holding. This work brings initial insights into asynchronous multimodal coordination as a core governing principle of proactive turn-taking negotiation.

items.title: CoDeTT: A Context-Aware Decision Benchmark for Turn-Taking Evaluation
items.authors: Huan Shen(Bairong Inc.); Yingao Wang(Bairong Inc.); Shangkun Huang(Bairong Inc.); Wei Zou(BRVoice Team); Yunzhang Chen(BRVoice Team)
items.abstract: Turn-taking modeling is fundamental to spoken dialogue systems, yet its evaluation remains fragmented and often limited to binary boundary detection under narrow interaction settings. Such protocols hinder systematic comparison and obscure model weaknesses across conversational conditions. We present CoDeTT, a context-aware decision benchmark for turn-taking evaluation. CoDeTT formulates turn-taking as a structured decision problem and constructs a multi-scenario dataset with fine-grained decision categories and controlled context variations. Under a unified evaluation protocol, we assess representative existing models and observe substantial performance disparities across decision types and interaction scenarios. CoDeTT provides a standardized benchmark for systematic and context-aware evaluation of turn-taking systems.

items.title: DualTurn: Learning Turn-Taking from Dual-Channel Generative Speech Pretraining
items.authors: Shangeth Rajaa(Anyreach AI)
items.abstract: Speech-to-speech models handle turn-taking naturally but offer limited tool-calling and reasoning, while production ASR-LLM-TTS pipelines have these capabilities yet rely on silence timeouts that make turn-taking unnatural. We present DualTurn, which narrows this gap through generative pretraining on dual-channel conversational audio. The model autoregressively generates both speakers' future audio, learning conversational dynamics without any labels, and is then fine-tuned to predict interpretable turn-taking signals that map directly to agent actions. DualTurn monitors both channels continuously, anticipating turn boundaries and producing five agent actions. On standard benchmarks, DualTurn (0.5B) outperforms both VAP on agent action prediction (wF1 0.633 vs. 0.389) and a 3.1B audio-text model on word-level prediction (AUC 0.930 vs. 0.880), anticipating turns earlier with fewer interruptions while running in real time on a CPU.

items.title: Endpoint Anticipation for Low-Latency Spoken Dialogue
items.authors: Sathvik Udupa(Brno University of Technology); Shinji Watanabe(Carnegie Mellon University); Petr Schwarz(Brno University of Technology); Jan Cernocky(Brno University of Technology)
items.abstract: While low-latency interaction is critical for spoken dialogue, cascaded architectures are often bottlenecked by reactive turn-completion detection. We propose Endpoint Anticipation, shifting from reactive detection to proactive forecasting of end-of-turn signals. Our speech-based model anticipates endpoints up to 2.56 seconds in advance, enabling speculative execution of LLM and TTS pipelines on partial context. We introduce metrics to quantify the trade-off between realized latency reduction and computational redundancy. Evaluation across conversational and task-oriented datasets shows our model consistently outperforms competitive VAP-based baselines. Integration with the Unmute framework demonstrates a 505 ms average latency reduction with a 28.4% increase in speculative computation, effectively masking sequential bottlenecks to enable complex reasoning in real-time speech-to-speech interaction.

items.title: Less can be More: What Aspects of Speech Drive End-of-Turn Detection
items.authors: Rini Sharon(Uniphore); Manickavela A(Uniphore); Kadri Hacioglu(Uniphore); Andreas Stolcke(Uniphore)
items.abstract: In conversational AI, detecting when a speaker has finished talking is crucial for natural turn-taking. While recent work incorporates semantics, the relative contribution of different modalities remains unclear. We present a controlled ablation of acoustic, prosodic, and semantic signals for streaming end-of-turn detection using a lightweight trimodal classifier. Under identical training conditions, the acoustic-prosodic combination achieves the best balance of accuracy and latency, achieving utterance F1 of 0.93 with 7.8% false alarms at 400ms median latency. Adding text increases premature detections without improving performance. Feature space analysis confirms that prosodic features have the strongest class separability, while text representations overlap substantially. These findings suggest that turn-taking is primarily conveyed through intonation and silence patterns rather than semantic completeness, enabling faster and more reliable systems without expensive text inference.

items.title: Uncovering Dimension-Specific Layer Preferences in Wav2Vec2 for Fine-Grained Perceptual Assessment of Dysarthric Speech
items.authors: Zihan Zhong(DeepNet Discovery Network; University of Auckland); Qianli Wang(DeepNet Discovery Network; University of Auckland); Satwinder Singh(DeepNet Discovery Network; University of Auckland); Clarion Mendes(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Mark Hasegawa-Johnson(University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign); Waleed Abdulla(DeepNet Discovery Network; University of Auckland); Seyed Reza Shahamiri(DeepNet Discovery Network; University of Auckland)
items.abstract: Fine-grained automatic dysarthric speech assessment can assist clinicians in providing targeted treatment. Yet, prior work often defaults to extracting features from a single self-supervised layer, potentially discarding relevant information. In this work, we first adapt the Wav2Vec2-Large encoder to dysarthric speech via unsupervised domain adaptation, then perform a layer-wise analysis to study layer preferences across 25 Darley-Aronson-Brown perceptual dimensions using the Speech Accessibility Project corpus. Our results show that the optimal layer varies across dimensions. We therefore fuse all layers via learnable scalar mixing to leverage complementary cues across layers, surpassing single-layer baselines. The learned weights reveal dimension-specific preferences aligned with speech-subsystem groupings, suggesting that matching representation depth to each dimension's acoustic-linguistic nature could be important for multi-dimensional dysarthric speech assessment.

items.title: Cross-lingual Retrieval-Augmented Classification for Dysarthria Severity Assessment
items.authors: Taeyoung Jeong(Sogang University); Insung Lee(Sogang University); Du-Seong Chang(Sogang University); Myoung-Wan Koo(Sogang University)
items.abstract: Automatic dysarthria severity assessment is limited by the scarcity of labeled pathological speech data. To address this, we propose Cross-lingual Retrieval-Augmented Classification (CRAC), which leverages speech from a different language via an align-retrieve-fuse pipeline. Supervised contrastive learning first shapes a severity-focused embedding space, then a vector database is built from the opposite-language corpus. During both training and inference, the classifier retrieves top-k references from the aligned space and fuses them with the input via cross-attention. Evaluated on Korean post-stroke and Italian ALS dysarthria datasets under a speaker-independent three-class protocol, CRAC achieves balanced accuracies of 87.3% on Korean and 86.7% on Italian, improving over monolingual baselines by 8.4 and 20.0 percentage points, respectively.

items.title: PathBench: Speech Intelligibility Benchmark for Automatic Pathological Speech Assessment
items.authors: Bence Mark Halpern(Nagoya University); Thomas Tienkamp(University of Cologne); Defne Abur(University of Groningen); Tomoki Toda(Nagoya University)
items.abstract: Automatic speech intelligibility assessment is crucial for monitoring speech disorders and therapy efficacy. However, existing methods are difficult to compare: research is fragmented across private datasets with inconsistent protocols. We introduce PathBench, a unified benchmark for pathological speech assessment using public datasets. We compare reference-free, reference-text, and reference-audio methods across three protocols (Matched Content, Extended, and Full) representing how a linguist (controlled stimuli) versus machine learning specialist (maximum data) would approach the same data. We establish benchmark baselines across six datasets, enabling systematic evaluation of future methodological advances, and introduce Dual-ASR Articulatory Precision (DArtP), achieving the highest average correlation among reference-free methods.

items.title: A Benchmark for Early-stage Parkinson's Disease Detection from Speech
items.authors: Terry Yi Zhong(Radboud University); Cristian Tejedor-Garcia(Radboud University); Khiet P. Truong(Radboud University); Janna Maas(Radboud University Medical Center); Louis ten Bosch(Radboud University); Bastiaan R. Bloem(Radboud University Medical Center)
items.abstract: Early-stage Parkinson's disease (EarlyPD) detection from speech is clinically meaningful yet underexplored, and published results are hard to compare because studies differ in datasets, languages, tasks, evaluation protocols, and EarlyPD definitions. To address this issue, we propose the first benchmark for speech-based EarlyPD detection, with a speaker-independent split designed for fair and replicable cross-method evaluation on researcher-accessible datasets. The benchmark covers three common speech tasks and evaluates methods under different training-resource settings. We also present multi-dimensional evaluation breakdowns by dataset, aggregation level, gender, and disease stage to support fine-grained comparisons and clinical adoption. Our results provide a replicable reference and actionable insights, encouraging the adoption of this publicly available benchmark to advance robust and clinically meaningful speech-based EarlyPD detection.

items.title: Harf-Speech: A Clinically Aligned Framework for Arabic Phoneme-Level Speech Assessment
items.authors: Asif Azad(Ministry of Defense, Saudi Arabia); MD Sadik Hossain Shanto(Ministry of Defense, Saudi Arabia); Mohammad Sadat Hossain(Ministry of Defense, Saudi Arabia); Bdour Alwuqaysi(Ministry of Defense, Saudi Arabia); Sabri Boughorbel(Ministry of Defense, Saudi Arabia); Yahya Bokhari(Ministry of Defense, Saudi Arabia); Abdulrhman Aljouie(Ministry of Defense, Saudi Arabia); Ayah Othman Sindi(Ability Center, Saudi Arabia); Ehsan Hoque(Ministry of Defense, Saudi Arabia; University of Rochester)
items.abstract: Automated phoneme-level pronunciation assessment is vital for scalable speech therapy and language learning, yet validated tools for Arabic remain scarce. We present Harf-Speech, a modular system scoring Arabic pronunciation at the phoneme level on a clinical scale. It combines an MSA phonetizer, a fine-tuned speech-to-phoneme model, Levenshtein alignment, and a blended scorer using longest common subsequence and edit-distance metrics. We fine-tune three ASR architectures on Arabic phoneme data and benchmark them with zero-shot multimodal models; the best, OmniASR-CTC-1B-v2, achieves 8.92% phoneme error rate. Three certified speech-language pathologists independently scored 40 utterances for clinical validation. Harf-Speech attains a Pearson correlation of 0.791 and ICC(2,1) of 0.659 with mean expert scores, outperforming existing end-to-end assessment frameworks. These results show Harf-Speech yields clinically aligned, interpretable scores comparable to inter-rater expert agreement.

items.title: What Does a Pathological Speech Assessment Model Know about Acoustic Features? A Case Study on Oral and Oropharyngeal Cancer Patients
items.authors: Tuan Nguyen(Avignon University); Corinne Fredouille(Avignon University); Alain Ghio(Aix-Marseille Univ); Muriel Lalain(Aix-Marseille Univ); Virginie Woisard(LNPL; Hôspital de Toulouse)
items.abstract: This work investigates the interpretability of a Wav2Vec 2.0-based speech intelligibility assessment model for oral and oropharyngeal cancer patients through canonical correlation analysis. By measuring the correlation between the model embeddings and eGeMAPS low-level descriptors (LLDs) as an interpretable reference, we analyze how acoustic information is encoded across the model layers. The analysis is conducted at two levels: individual LLDs layer-wise, and group-level: prosodic, spectral, and voice quality. Results show that the learned representations are most strongly correlated with spectral and prosodic features, with the first MFCC coefficient yielding the highest correlations across all layers. At the group level, spectral and prosodic groups achieve correlations of 0.77 and 0.71 respectively, while voice quality reaches 0.65. Beyond model interpretability, this work also offers practical guidance on acoustic feature selection for pathological speech assessment.

items.title: TaigiSpeech: A Low-Resource Real-World Speech Intent Dataset with Scalable Data Mining In-the-Wild
items.authors: Kai-Wei Chang(Massachusetts Institute of Technology); Yi-Cheng Lin(National Taiwan University); Huang-Cheng Chou(University of Southern California); Wenze Ren(National Taiwan University); Yu-Han Huang(National Taiwan University); Yun-Shao Tsai(National Taiwan University); Chien-Cheng Chen(National Taiwan University); Yu Tsao(Academia Sinica); Yuan-Fu Liao(National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University); Shrikanth Narayanan(University of Southern California); James Glass(Massachusetts Institute of Technology); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University; National Taiwan University Artiﬁcial Intelligence Center of Research Excellence)
items.abstract: Speech technologies have advanced rapidly and serve diverse populations worldwide. However, many languages remain underrepresented due to limited resources. In this paper, we introduce TaigiSpeech, a real-world speech intent dataset in Taiwanese Taigi (aka Taiwanese Hokkien / Southern Min), which is a low-resource and primarily spoken language. The dataset is collected from older adults, comprising 21 speakers with a total of 3k utterances. It is designed for practical intent detection scenarios, including healthcare and home assistant applications. To address the scarcity of labeled data, we explore two data mining strategies with two levels of supervision: keyword match data mining with LLM pseudo labeling via an intermediate language and an audio-visual framework that leverages multimodal cues with minimal textual supervision. This design enables scalable dataset construction for low-resource and unwritten spoken languages. TaigiSpeech will be released under the CC BY 4.0 license to facilitate broad adoption and research on low-resource and unwritten languages. The project website and the dataset can be found on https://kwchang.org/taigispeech.

items.title: Hallucination Benchmark for Speech Foundation Models
items.authors: Alkis Koudounas(Politecnico di Torino); Moreno La Quatra(Kore University of Enna); Manuel Giollo(Amazon AGI); Sabato Marco Siniscalchi(Università degli Studi di Palermo); Elena Baralis(Politecnico di Torino)
items.abstract: This work advances the detection of hallucinations in automatic speech recognition (ASR) by introducing SHALLOW, the first benchmark that categorizes ASR hallucinations along four dimensions of analysis: lexical, phonetic, morphological, and semantic. Standard ASR metrics, such as Word Error Rate (WER), fail to capture the distinctions necessary to separate hallucinations from phonetic inaccuracies, leaving a critical gap in model evaluation. SHALLOW addresses this limitation by providing targeted metrics within each dimension, yielding interpretable profiles of model behavior. Evaluations across diverse architectures and domains show that SHALLOW strongly correlates with WER under high recognition quality; however, this correlation degrades as WER increases, exposing fine-grained error patterns that aggregate metrics overlook. By disentangling hallucination phenomena from general recognition errors, SHALLOW enables targeted diagnosis of model weaknesses.

items.title: INSPIRE: A Benchmark for Instruction-Aware Speech Retrieval
items.authors: Chen-An Li(National Taiwan University); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University; NTU AI-CoRE)
items.abstract: Existing speech retrieval systems rely on fixed similarity matching and cannot adapt to diverse user intents. We introduce INSPIRE, the first benchmark for instruction-aware speech retrieval, in which natural-language instructions dynamically specify relevance criteria, including semantic content, speaker identity, speaking style, environmental sounds, and their combinations. We evaluate four retrieval paradigms: large audio-language models, cascaded pipelines, self-supervised speech models, and contrastive audio-language models. Our results reveal that no current method robustly handles all retrieval intents. Text-based approaches perform relatively better at semantic retrieval but struggle with paralinguistic attributes, while speech-based models are moderately better at capturing acoustic properties but falter at following instructions. These findings highlight the need for unified architectures capable of instruction-aware speech retrieval.

items.title: StanceBench: A Benchmark for Audio LLM-Based Interpersonal Stance Evaluation from Speech
items.authors: Yuzhe Wang(Johns Hopkins University); Thomas Thebaud(Johns Hopkins University); Jennifer Hu(Johns Hopkins University); Jesús Villalba-Lopez(Johns Hopkins University); Venkatesh Ravichandran(Amazon AGI); Georgi Tinchev(Amazon Research); Najim Dehak(Johns Hopkins University); Laureano Moro-Velázquez(Johns Hopkins University)
items.abstract: Speech-to-speech dialogue models increasingly depend on prosody and interactional nuance to convey social intent, yet benchmarks for these cues remain limited. We introduce StanceBench, a benchmark for measuring interpersonal stance in conversational speech and evaluating audio-capable LLMs as automated judges. Using the Seamless Interaction corpus, StanceBench (1) specifies 9 stance dimensions via role-prompt poles, (2) standardizes single-speaker and interaction-based evaluations, and (3) reports LLM-as-a-judge robustness, bias, and stance inference. Across evaluated stances, empathy and politeness are the easiest. Warmth and assertiveness are moderately separable with positivity skew/asymmetry. Honesty is the hardest and shows high prompt order bias, consistent with needing cross-turn evidence. Attentiveness is separable but aligns weakly with humans. Interaction stances are more context-sensitive, with threshold gaps and high variance, especially conflict regulation.

items.title: NVV-SuperBench: Beyond Words, Beyond Quality—Benchmarking Nonverbal Vocalizations in Speech Generation
items.authors: Liumeng Xue(Nanjing University; The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Weizhen Bian(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Jiahao Pan(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Wenxuan Wu(The Chinese University of Hong Kong); Yilin Ren(University of Science and Technology Beijing); Boyi Kang(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology); Jingbin Hu(Northwestern Polytechnical University); Ziyang Ma(Shanghai Jiao Tong University); Shuai Wang(Nanjing University); Xinyuan Qian(University of Science and Technology Beijing); Hung-yi Lee(National Taiwan University); Yike Guo(The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology)
items.abstract: Nonverbal vocalizations (NVVs), such as laughing, sighing, and sobbing, are essential for human-like speech, yet standardized evaluation rarely jointly assesses whether systems generate the intended NVVs, place them correctly, and keep them salient without harming speech. We present NVV-SuperBench, a bilingual English/Chinese benchmark for speech generation with NVVs. It provides a unified 45-type taxonomy and a multi-axis protocol beyond conventional speech quality assessment, evaluating NVV-specific controllability, placement, and perceptual salience. We benchmark 15 speech generation systems spanning prompt-based and tag-based control paradigms, using objective metrics, human listening tests, and LLM-based multi-rater evaluation. Results show that NVV controllability often decouples from speech quality, while low-SNR oral cues and long-duration affective NVVs remain bottlenecks. NVV-SuperBench highlights current gaps and supports progress toward more human-like speech generation.

items.title: How Frequency Band Importance Affects Neural Network Predictions and Human Perception for Speech Quality Assessment
items.authors: Ada Lamba(The Ohio State University); Donald Williamson(The Ohio State University)
items.abstract: Audio quality assessment models are often used for evaluating speech enhancement and noise suppression approaches. However, recent work has shown that network predictions do not always correlate well with human predictions. Explainability could help developers and users of these tools identify potential error and data bias, which would expedite development. In this work, we use Shapley additive explanations, partial dependence plots, and perturbation analysis to determine the influential frequency bands for three quality assessment models. We then conduct a listening study to determine if human perception is sensitive to the same factors as these networks. Our results show that both networks and humans are more sensitive to detrimental factors than beneficial ones. Further, the networks focus on a small portion of the input which corresponds to low frequency bands. Our work represents a step towards unifying explainability for both humans and networks.

items.title: Vowel Allophony Improves Maximum-Likelihood Classification of Warlpiri Consonants
items.authors: Coralie Cram(UCLA); John McGahay(UCLA); Megha Sundara(UCLA)
items.abstract: Australian languages typically have a large number of place contrasts and relatively few manner contrasts. We investigated the acoustic cues that native speakers of Warlpiri, an Australian language with stops in five places of articulation, could use to distinguish them. Using a maximum-likelihood classifier, we show that acoustic cues intrinsic to consonants are not sufficient for this purpose. Adding information from consonant-extrinsic acoustic cues in adjacent vowels improved consonant classification for both CV and VC sequences. In both CVs and VCs, consonant classification benefited the most from allophony in formants at midpoints of adjacent vowels. We discuss the implications of our results and the potential of using maximum-likelihood classifiers for generating predictions based on probabilistic models of speech perception for low resource languages.

items.title: Towards Robust Ultrasound-based Silent Speech Recognition Learning Physics-Aware and Context-Rich Representations
items.authors: Hongyu Wen(National University of Defense Technology); Yi Su(National University of Defense Technology); Yudong Yang(Chinese Academy of Sciences); Siwen Guo(National University of Defense Technology); Qisheng Xu(National University of Defense Technology); Kele Xu(National University of Defense Technology)
items.abstract: Silent Speech Recognition (SSR) decodes linguistic intent from non-acoustic biological signals, where Ultrasound Tongue Imaging (UTI) serves as a pivotal non-invasive modality. However, imaging artifacts and complex temporal dependencies make extracting robust features from UTI sequences challenging. To address these issues, we propose a framework for learning physics-aware and context-rich representations. Specifically, a temporal clustering strategy is employed to downsample sequences while preserving critical context, complemented by a physics-aware augmentation that enforces model robustness against imaging perturbations. Furthermore, temporal masking and a hybrid architecture integrating 3D convolutional networks with bidirectional recurrent layers are utilized to promote spatiotemporal representation learning. Our method significantly outperforms baselines, validating that modeling physical consistency and structural completeness is essential for advancing robust UTI-based SSR.

items.title: Acoustic-to-Articulatory Inversion of Clean Speech Using an MRI-Trained Model
items.authors: Sofiane Azzouz(Loria)
items.abstract: Articulatory acoustic inversion reconstructs vocal tract shapes from speech. Real-time magnetic resonance imaging (rt-MRI) allows simultaneous acquisition of both the acoustic speech signal and articulatory information. Besides the complexity of rt-MRI acquisition, the recorded audio is heavily corrupted by scanner noise and requires denoising to be usable. For practical use, it must be possible to invert speech recorded without MRI noise. In this study, we investigate the use of speech recorded in a clean acoustic environment as an alternative to denoised MRI speech. To this end we compare two signals from the same speaker with identical sentences which are aligned using phonetic segmentation. A model trained on denoised MRI speech is evaluated on both denoised MRI and clean speech. We also assess a model trained and tested only on clean speech. Results show that clean speech supports articulatory inversion effectively, achieving an RMSE of 1.56 mm, close to MRI-based performance.

items.title: UniVoice: Unifying Autoregressive ASR and Flow-Matching based TTS with Large Language Models
items.authors: Wenhao Guan(Xiamen University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Zhikang Niu(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Ziyue Jiang(Zhejiang University); Kaidi Wang(Xiamen University); Peijie Chen(Xiamen University); Qingyang Hong(Xiamen University); Xie Chen(Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Innovation Institute); Lin Li(Xiamen University)
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become dominant in both Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS), but existing frameworks treat these tasks as isolated, overlooking inherent synergies. While discrete tokenization enables joint modeling, information loss compromises accuracy and synthesis quality. To address the limitations, we propose UniVoice, a unified LLM integrating ASR and TTS via continuous representations. Beyond discrete tokens, UniVoice preserves acoustic details for robust autoregressive recognition and high-fidelity flow-matching generation. To bridge architectural divergence between understanding and generation, we introduce a dual-attention masking mechanism to dynamically switch between causal masks for ASR and bidirectional masks for TTS. Additionally, text-prefix guided speech infilling ensures superior zero-shot voice cloning. Experimental results show UniVoice achieves competitive or superior performance to state-of-the-art single-task models, marking a significant step toward end-to-end speech interaction systems. The code and model weights are available at https://github. com/gwh22/UniVoice.

items.title: How do word frequency and syllable surprisal affect response time and acoustic duration in sentence formulation?
items.authors: Ivan Yuen(Saarland Univeristy); Bernd Möbius(Saarland University); Bistra Andreeva(Saarland University); Mitko Sabev(Saarland University)
items.abstract: Although predictability effects have been shown to affect acoustic realization (e.g., [1 - 8]) at different linguistic levels, they are mostly based on variation of predictability at a specific linguistic level. Yet linguistic levels are embedded within one another. ‘Frequency of occurrence’ is one type of predictability, which could occur at the level of word (word frequency) and syllable (syllable frequency). The current study explored such cross-level interaction on response time and acoustic vowel duration in German, in the context of the psycholinguistic model of speech production in [14]. We hypothesized an additive effect; however, our findings revealed selective interaction, depending on whether the word is mono- or di-syllabic. These results challenge the assumption of ‘discrete, staged and serial’ processing across levels in [14].

items.title: Extreme Few-Shot Phoneme Discovery for Indigenous Australian and Pacific Languages via Typological Transfer Learning
items.authors: Prasanth Yadla(Independent Researcher)
items.abstract: Indigenous Australian and Pacific languages face extinction, and many have fewer than ten hours of transcribed speech. Conventional acoustic unit discovery often assumes over 100 hours of unlabeled audio--far beyond what is available for endangered languages. We propose an extreme few-shot phoneme discovery framework that operates on under one hour of audio, leveraging typological transfer from high-resource Austronesian languages through a Vector-Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE). We introduce Typological Anchor Selection (TAS), which selects optimal source languages based on phonetic inventory overlap. Evaluated on three endangered language datasets, our approach improves Normalized Mutual Information by 18.8% and cluster purity by 15.6% over multilingual self-supervised baselines. This provides a scalable path for rapid language documentation and revitalization.

items.title: Lexical stress-conditioned spatiotemporal gestural coordination in L2 English
items.authors: Paul McGuire(Macquarie University; National Tsing Hua University); Michael Proctor(Macquarie University); Feng-fan Hsieh(National Tsing Hua University); Yueh-chin Chang(National Tsing Hua University)
items.abstract: This study examines the articulatory realisation of lexical stress in L2 English produced by speakers of Taiwanese Mandarin, a language without a perceptually salient lexical stress contrast. Electromagnetic articulography was used to record articulatory data, and multivariate functional principal component analysis with landmark-based temporal registration was applied to analyse the spatiotemporal coordination of articulatory gestures across a syllable. Accentedness ratings were used to contextualise inter-speaker differences in stress-condition separation in FPCA score space. Four of the six speakers showed evidence of separation between stress conditions, whereas the two speakers judged to have the strongest perceived foreign accents did not.

items.title: Automated Measurement of Geniohyoid Muscle Thickness During Speech Using Deep Learning and UltrasoundAutomated Measurement of Geniohyoid Muscle Thickness During Speech Using Deep Learning and Ultrasound
items.authors: Alisher Myrgyyassov(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Bruce Xiao Wang(Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yu Sun(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Shuming Huang(Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Zhen Song(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Min Ney Wong(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University); Yongping Zheng(The Hong Kong Polytechnic University)
items.abstract: Manual measurement of muscle morphology from ultrasound during speech is time-consuming and limits large-scale studies. We present SMMA, a fully automated framework combining deep learning segmentation with skeleton-based thickness quantification for analyzing geniohyoid (GH) muscle dynamics. Validation demonstrates near-human-level accuracy (Dice: 0.9037, MAE: 0.53 mm, r = 0.901). Application to Cantonese vowel production (N = 11) reveals systematic patterns: /a:/ shows significantly greater GH thickness (7.29 mm) than /i:/ (5.95 mm, p < 0.001, Cohen's d > 1.3), suggesting greater GH activation during the production of /a:/ than /i:/, consistent with its role in mandibular depression. Sex differences (5-8% greater in males) reflect anatomical scaling. SMMA achieves expert-validated accuracy while eliminating the need for manual annotation, enabling scalable investigations of speech motor control and objective assessment of speech/swallowing disorders.

items.title: Articulatory Dynamics using Physical Vocal-tract Models
items.authors: Takayuki Arai(Sophia University)
items.abstract: Visualizing and modeling the vocal tract during speech production is crucial in several speech-related areas, including phonetics and phonology, education in phonetics and speech science, and speech pathology. Once the observation and analysis are done, it becomes crucial to evaluate the “synthesized” speech outputs from the model. While speech synthesis is often performed on a computer, physical vocal-tract models provide an alternative and intuitive approach. Some physical models are static and their configurations cannot be altered. Others are dynamic, allowing us to change their configurations and easily adjust the articulatory parameters. Here, a physically dynamic model was tested to produce given words with different sets of articulatory timings. The model was able to show dynamic aspects of speech from the articulatory phonology point of view.

items.title: AcoustEmo: An Utterance-Aware Acoustic Q-Former for Open-Vocabulary Emotion Reasoning
items.authors: Liyun Zhang(The University of Tokyo); Xuanmeng Sha(The University of Osaka); Shuqiong Wu(The University of Osaka); Fengkai Liu(The University of Osaka)
items.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) excel in Open-Vocabulary (OV) emotion recognition but often neglect fine-grained acoustic modeling. Existing methods typically use global audio encoders, failing to capture subtle, local temporal dynamics like micro-prosody and intonation shifts within individual utterances. To address this, we propose AcoustEmo, a time-sensitive MLLM featuring a novel Utterance-Aware Acoustic Q-Former. Our approach utilizes a timestamp-synchronized sliding window to dynamically extract segment-level audio tokens instead of coarse global representations. This enables the model to explicitly trace the temporal evolution of subtle acoustic clues and capture deep contextual dependencies in dialogues. Experiments on the Explainable Multimodal Emotion Recognition (EMER) task show that AcoustEmo effectively enhances complex emotion reasoning, outperforming baselines overall while maintaining robust contextual accuracy.

items.title: Edge–Cloud Collaborative Speech Emotion Captioning via Token-Level Speculative Decoding in Audio-Language Models
items.authors: Xiangyuan Xue(University of Auckland); Jiajun Lu(University of Melbourne); Yan Gao(University of Cambridge); Gongping Huang(Wuhan University); Ting Dang(University of Melbourne); Hong Jia(University of Auckland)
items.abstract: Speech Emotion Captioning (SEC) leverages large audio-language models to generate rich, context-aware affective descriptions from speech. However, real-world deployment remains challenging due to the substantial computational demands on resource-constrained edge devices and the privacy risks of transmitting biometric audio. While smaller audio-language models enable efficient on-device SEC, their limited capacity often weakens subtle paralinguistic modeling and fine-grained affective grounding. We propose an edge-cloud collaborative framework based on Uncertainty-Guided Speculative Decoding (UGSD). A lightweight edge model drafts captions locally, and only high-uncertainty token blocks are selectively escalated to a stronger cloud verifier for validation. Experiments on the MER2024 benchmark demonstrate substantial BLEU improvements up to 62.7%. UGSD further achieves 1.4× lower latency and 8.5× higher token throughput compared to an edge-only model. These results empirically characterize the quality-efficiency-privacy trade-off in deployable SEC systems.

items.title: Disentangling Reasoning in Large Audio-Language Models for Ambiguous Emotion Prediction
items.authors: Xiaofeng Yu(University of Auckland); Jiaheng Dong(The University of Melbourne); Jean Honorio(The University of Melbourne; ARC OPTIMA); Abhirup Ghosh(University of Birmingham); Hong Jia(University of Auckland); Ting Dang(The University of Melbourne)
items.abstract: Speech emotion recognition plays an important role in various applications. However, most existing approaches predict a single emotion label, oversimplifying the inherently ambiguous nature of human emotional expression. Recent large audio-language models show promise in generating richer outputs, but their reasoning ability for ambiguous emotional understanding remains limited. In this work, we reformulate ambiguous emotion recognition as a distributional reasoning problem and present the first systematic study of ambiguity-aware reasoning in LALMs. Our framework comprises two complementary components: an ambiguity-aware objective that aligns predictions with human perceptual distributions, and a structured ambiguity-aware chain-of-thought supervision that guides reasoning over emotional cues. Experiments on IEMOCAP and CREMA-D demonstrate consistent improvements across SFT, DPO, and GRPO training strategies.

items.title: AdaLTM: Adaptive Layer-wise Task Vector Merging for Categorical Speech Emotion Recognition with ASR Knowledge Integration
items.authors: Chia-Yu Lee(National Tsing Hua University); Huang-Cheng Chou(University of Southern California); Tzu-Quan Lin(National Taiwan University); Yuanchao Li(University of Edinburgh); Ya-Tse Wu(National Tsing Hua University); Shrikanth Narayanan(University of Southern California); Chi-Chun Lee(National Tsing Hua University)
items.abstract: Integrating Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) into Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) enhances modeling by providing linguistic context. However, conventional feature fusion faces performance bottlenecks, and multi-task learning often suffers from optimization conflicts. While task vectors and model merging have addressed such conflicts in NLP and CV, their potential in speech tasks remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose an Adaptive Layer-wise Task Vector Merging (AdaLTM) framework based on WavLM-Large. Instead of joint optimization, we extract task vectors from in-domain ASR and SER models fine-tuned on emotion datasets. These vectors are integrated into a frozen base model using layer-wise learnable coefficients. This strategy enables depth-aware balancing of linguistic and paralinguistic knowledge across transformer layers without gradient interference. Experiments on the MSP-Podcast demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively mitigates conflicts between ASR and SER.

items.title: SETEAB: Multiscale approach with Squeeze-and-Excitation Temporal Enhanced Aware Block for Speech Emotion Recognition
items.authors: Duy Vo(University of Science; Vietnam National University); Kiet Anh Hoang(University of Science; Vietnam National University; UNEY); Hao Do(University of Science; Vietnam National University)
items.abstract: This paper proposes a novel lightweight multiscale architecture for speech emotion recognition (SER) with three key innovations. First, a depthwise convolution-based subsampling module is introduced to reduce model size and computation while preserving salient emotional cues. Second, a Squeeze-and-Excitation block is integrated to enhance channel-wise recalibration and improve representation robustness. Third, a new Temporal Enhanced Aware Block is designed to strengthen temporal dependency modeling and produce more discriminative emotion-aware features. The proposed model is explicitly designed to jointly improve compactness, recognition performance, and generalizability. Experiments on benchmark SER datasets show that our method achieves higher accuracy with reduced computational complexity, while also delivering stronger cross-corpus performance than most recent advanced networks for SER.

items.title: How Language-Independent Are Emotional Attributes? A Study on Training Data Scaling and Cross-Lingual Generalization
items.authors: Dániel Halmai(University of Szeged); Gábor Gosztolya(University of Szeged; HUN-REN–SZTE Research Group on Artificial Intelligence)
items.abstract: Current state-of-the-art Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) systems rely on lots of training data, which is available only for a few languages such as English. For low-resource languages, using a cross-lingual model or adapting it to the target language might be an alternative to training a mono-lingual model from scratch. However, it is not clear what constitutes a 'low-resource', i.e. where model adaptation loses its edge over the mono-lingual approach. We investigate this topic by training and adapting several SER models on English and Mandarin data, focusing on the emotional attributes of arousal, valence and dominance. Our results show that, for arousal, model adaptation is beneficial even with two hours of data, while for valence 10-20 hours of adaptation material is required to match the performance of a mono-lingual model trained with 100 hours of data. This indicates that task-specific model adaptation may be an effective approach in low-resource speech emotion recognition problems.

items.title: SISER: Speaker-Invariant Speech Emotion Recognition with Entropy-Based Adversarial Training
items.authors: Eunseo Choi(Korea University); Hyunku Kang(Korea University); Chanwoo Kim(Korea University)
items.abstract: Speech emotion recognition (SER) faces two fundamental challenges: scarcity of labeled data and inter-speaker variability, both of which hinder generalization of emotion recognition systems. While prior adversarial approaches address speaker variability, they fall short in leveraging powerful pre-trained representations. We propose SISER (Speaker-Invariant Speech Emotion Recognition), integrating wav2vec 2.0 as a feature encoder and ECAPA-TDNN as a speaker discriminator within an entropy-based adversarial training scheme. wav2vec 2.0 provides rich self-supervised representations that alleviate dependency on large labeled datasets, while ECAPA-TDNN enables suppression of speaker identity via a stronger adversarial signal than shallow classifiers. Evaluated on IEMOCAP, SISER achieves a UA of 60.63%, outperforming the baseline (51.15%) and wav2vec 2.0 without speaker suppression (56.46%), with ablation emphasizing that the choice of speaker classifier architecture is a key factor.

items.title: Robust Audio-Visual Emotion Recognition via Conditional Transformer U-Nets with Frequency-Injected Visual Stream
items.authors: Hanwook Chung(Faurecia IRYStec)
items.abstract: We present a convolutional transformer (CTr)-based dual U-Net for robust audio-visual emotion recognition (AVER) in noisy and reverberation environments. Each CTr U-Net encoder learns compact, modality-specific bottleneck representations that capture contextual and temporal-spatial cues from audio and visual inputs, while a fusion-based emotion decoder predicts emotional states from the joint bottleneck features. Emotion-conditioned auxiliary decoders reconstruct intermediate features to enhance supervision and consistency. The audio stream incorporates an inverse filtering-based front-end, while the visual stream employs frequency-injected spatial-spectral modeling to better capture facial dynamics. Experiments demonstrate improved robustness and accuracy compared to existing unimodal and multimodal benchmarks.

items.title: Diffusion Bridge Learning Between Overfitted and Underfitted Representations for speech emotion recognition
items.authors: Shi-wook Lee(AIST)
items.abstract: Robust recognition of human emotions from speech remains difficult under domain and language shift because neural encoders often overfit to dataset-specific acoustic cues. This paper proposes a diffusion-based representation-space training framework that reshapes learned representations toward class-centered geometry. The model introduces class prototypes as anchors and learns stochastic sample–prototype transformations using a conditional denoising diffusion process with paired alignment, cycle consistency, and classifier-based regularization. Experiments on cross-lingual emotion recognition between English and Japanese show consistent improvements in weighted average recall. The proposed method achieves up to +6.42 percentage points in English-to-Japanese evaluation and +4.00 percentage points in Japanese-to-English evaluation, demonstrating improved robustness to cross-language domain shift.
